pdfinfo.title: Armors and weapons Aesthetics and Decoration V2024.12

pages.text:
1. Definition and general requirements
         Armors and weapons aesthetics are very important for the fighters' appearance and sports
         representation. The development of our sport will be easier with well-maintained and properly
         finished armor and weapons. Crafting armor and its parts is a process mostly made by hand with the
         help of different hand tools such as hammers and files, even during the surfacing process and
         polishing. Thus, it is not rare to find such traces on artifacts, even in the corners of a highly polished
         armor.

    1.1. The following aesthetics are allowed:
            ● Matte polish (see page 4)
            ● Satin Polish (see page 7)
            ● Mirror Polish (see page 9)
            ● Blackening and Bluing (see page 11)

    1.2. All types of aesthetics must respect the following requirements
             ● Be based on historical sources.
             ● Be homogenous regarding the whole set of armor: it is not allowed to mix different aesthetics
                in the same armor set unless specifically written in the specific requirements.
             ● The steel surface does not present strong forging remains, big filing traces, and modern
                grinding marks.
             ● Must be properly polished, any highly unpolished armor part is denied.
             ● Must be free of rust.

    1.3. Decoration
         An armor can be decorated with different methods, such as
            ● etching
            ● engraving
            ● plating and gilding
         Helmets can be decorated with the medieval spirit, with crest, torse, burlets or orle for example.

         Example of burlet:


                                                        Picture from Age of Craft ©




    1.4. Painted armor
         As the topic of painted armors is very controversial among armor experts, historical sources can’t
         stand a clear position about painted armor. We have historical sources for late-15th century helmets
         (mainly Sallets) but nothing relevant for the 14th century nor for armor parts. Therefore, any painted
         armor metal part, metal buckler or weapon is denied.




Armors and weapons Aesthetics and Decoration                                              3

2. Matte Polish

    2.1. Matte polish definition and sources
         A basic polishing method, widely used during the Middle Ages. Its appearance is flat and gray, and
         subtle marks from the polishing process are still visible. A utilitarian finish that hides scratches and
         holds a protective oil film well. The basic and most common finish is the matte polish. It is
         recommended for all types of 14th and 15th century armor and weapons.

         It is approved for 14th-century, Transitional armors and 15th-century armors.




                         Armet, on display at the Metropolitan Museum of Arts (MET) - 1440 - New York (USA)




    2.2. Specific requirements
           ● The whole armor or weapon must be matte polished.
           ● It is denied to have an armor set mixing matte polish with other aesthetics.
           ● Matte polish can be used with other decoration techniques, such as etching, engraving,
               gilding or plating.

3. Satin Polish

    3.1. Definition and sources
         Satin polish has a semi-reflective surface with a subdued sheen, the polishing marks are small and
         only visible upon close inspection. A practical polishing method that balances functionality with a
         refined appearance. Armors are polished with multiple grinding grits to obtain an intermediary
         reflective finish. It is not as shiny as mirror polishing.

         It is approved for 14th-century, Transitional armors and 15th-century armors.




                                Montefeltro Altarpiece by Piero della Francesca - 1472 - Italy
                                       Note: the helmet in this art is mirror polished




Armors and weapons Aesthetics and Decoration                                                     7

3.2. Specific requirements
            ● The whole armor must be satin polished or a mix of satin and mirror polished.
            ● It is denied to have an armor set mixing matte polishing parts with satin polishing parts.
            ● It is denied to have an armor set mixing black/blued polishing parts with satin polishing parts.
            ● Satin polish can be used with other decoration techniques, such as etching, engraving,
                gilding or plating.

4. Mirror Polish

    4.1. Mirror polish definition and sources
         A late-period polishing technique that gained popularity in the 15th century. Metal plates are polished
         with progressively finer grit until polishing marks are not visible, resulting in a reflective sheen. This
         finish requires high maintenance to keep it looking its best. Armors are polished with multiple
         grinding grits reaching into the 1000 grid to obtain a beautiful reflective finish.

         It is approved for 14th-century, Transitional armors and 15th-century armors..

                                              Sigismund von Tirol




                        Armor of Sigismund von Tirol, Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien - 1484 - Austria



    4.2. Specific requirements
            ● The whole armor must be satin polished or a mix of satin and mirror polished.
            ● It is denied to have an armor set mixing black/blued polishing parts with mirror polishing
                parts.
            ● Mirror polish can be used with other decoration techniques, such as etching, engraving,
                gilding or plating.

5. Blackening and Bluing
    5.1. Blackening and Bluing definition and sources
         Finishing method appearing in the mid-15th century sources, the metal plates are carefully heated to
         high temperatures to obtain a black or blue finish by treating the steel with oils.

         It is approved for 15th-century armors.
         It is denied for 14th-century and Transitional armors.

         Acceptable methods of blackening/Bluing are as followed:
            ● Temperature Bluing: The metal plates are carefully heated to adequate temperatures to
                obtain a blue oxide finish on the surface of the steel.
            ● Oil Blackening: This technique involves applying oils, such as linseed oil, to steel, which is
                then baked in an oven or applied to heated steel at relatively low temperatures. The process
                results in a deep black, protective finish. However, it requires regular touch-ups to maintain
                its appearance and protective qualities.
            ● Chemical blackening/bluing: Modern chemicals normally intended for use on firearms are
                permitted for armor. Hot-blue treatment is preferred, as it results in a deeper and more
                durable finish, but be mindful of how this could affect heat-treated steel. Cold-blue can be
                repeatedly applied to darken the surface of the steel and also to touch up hot-blued steel.




           Greenwich Armour replica (1595) Plates formed by Robert MacPherson & Jeff Wasson, decoration and finishing by Chris

5.2. Specific requirements
            ● The whole armor must be of the same method of blackening/bluing.
            ● It is denied to have an armor set mixing black/blued polishing parts with other aesthetics.
            ● Blackening/bluing finish can be used with other decoration techniques, such as etching,
                engraving, gilding, or plating.
            ● It is denied to use paint to reproduce a black/blued finish.

6. Decorations
    6.1. Definition and sources
         Armors were often decorated with different methods to display the owner’s status. The following
         decoration methods are documented by historical sources: etching, engraving, plating and gilding.
         Helmets were decorated with fabric or metal elements such as crest, burlet, torse and orle.


        It is approved for 14th-century armors, Transitional armors and 15th-century armors.




                Sir William Phelip, Lord Bardolph - 1441 - England




                                                                     BL Royal 20 C VII Chroniques de France ou de St Denis
                                                                     - 1380/1400 - France




                Late 14th century, MET Museum




Armors and weapons Aesthetics and Decoration                                                         14

6.2. Specific requirements
         Decoration must be based on historical sources. It is allowed to combine different decorations in a
         coherent way. Any decoration must not represent any offensive symbols, words, or sentence of any
         type. All political messages must not be used as decoration on armor and weapons. Any logo must
         be stylized to reach the middle-ages aesthetics and designs.

    6.3. The following decorations techniques are allowed:
            ● Etching: It is allowed to etch historical symbols and written words with etching techniques.
                Armor parts and weapons can be decorated this way.

            ●   Engraving: It is allowed to engrave historical symbols and written words with engraving
                techniques. Engraving can be done by hand or mechanically. Armor parts and weapons can
                be decorated this way.

            ●   Plating: It is allowed to decorate the edges of an armor part with metal plates. The following
                materials can be used:
                   ○ Copper
                   ○ Brass
                   ○ Gold
                   ○ Silver
                   ○ And any other metal that can be documented by historical sources.

            ●   Gilding: It is allowed to use gilding as a decoration on armor and weapons. The following
                materials can be used:
                   ○ Copper
                   ○ Brass
                   ○ Gold
                   ○ Silver
                   ○ And any other metal that can be documented by historical sources.

            ●   Helmet decorations: it is allowed to decorate a helmet in the medieval spirit. It must be
                based on historical sources. Any textile or leather part must conform with the Textiles and
                Leather document.

7. Repairs

    7.1. Definition and sources
         Armors were sometimes repaired to increase its durability. In the Middle Ages, the most common way
         to repair an armor was to rivet a metal plate from beneath. From a buhurt point of view, it will be
         important to respect period techniques for visible repairs. It is approved for 14th-century armors,
         Transitional armors, and 15th-century armors.




    7.2. Specific requirements
      ● Visible repairs must be executed with period techniques, for example with a riveted patch
         installed on the inside of the armor part and riveted.
      ● Repairs must be clean and not dangerous for other equipment elements.
      ● Any modern reparation is allowed if properly concealed. Any type of welding must be
         grinded/filed and polished on the outside.




Armors and weapons Aesthetics and Decoration                                         17
